newsitem.title: USA: NYC transit union approves pact, Giuliani objects.
newsitem.headline: NYC transit union approves pact, Giuliani objects.

text.p: New York transit workers said on Tuesday they approved a new, no-layoff pact, which includes a controversial provision to let welfare recipients work as cleaners, with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

However, Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has disapproved of the pact in part because he was not consulted by the agency in advance about its plans to have people on welfare clean subway trains, buses, and stations, showed no sign of backing down.

The Republican mayor has vigorously objected to the new contract even though he is advocates workfare programs. New York City now has around 35,000 welfare recipients enrolled in a Work Experience Program, which means they work for the city in return for their benefits.
"We have no comment on the Metropolitan Transportation Authority contract itself. People can evaluate the financial aspects for themselves," said Colleen Roche, a spokeswoman for Giuliani.

"With specific regard to the Work Experience Program, there is no agreement with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, and we do not anticipate any agreement with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority in the future."

How the agency plans to resolve the dispute with Giuliani was not immediatlely clear. The chairman of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, Virgil Conway, through a spokesman said only "We are very pleased," referring additional calls for comment to the mayor.

Although the union's contract had another year left, fears of layoffs prompted by the MTA's suggestion it might need to cut costs by as much as $350 million in the last three year's of its five-year plan helped push the union into early talks.
When the new contract was drafted, the agency's chairman pointed out that it would help the MTA cut costs, avoiding both layoffs and a fare hike.

The new labor contract, which was strongly opposed by a dissident group of the union, was approved by a margin of 773, with 8,183 voting in favor, and 7,410 against, according to Jim Gannon, a Transport Workers Union Local 100 spokesman.
He added that he expected the new contract, which covers the union's 33,000 members and expires on December 15, 1999, to go into effect immediately.

The pact calls for eliminating through attrition as many as 500 of 2,800 cleaning positions, opening the door for workfare participants. The move is expected to save the agency around $20 million a year, while another $40 million would be saved on a contribution to the union's medical plan, which has a surplus.
The mayor has not been backed by the Pataki Administration, which also favors expanding workfare programs, in his fight with the state agency.

Gov. George Pataki said he supported the labor agreement when it was proposed because it would not only make the transit system cleaner but give welfare recipients useful experience that would help them gain permanent jobs.
